subject: Ingress pattern selection for Crescent Labs private deployment — peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN
messages:
From: Alex Soto <alex.soto@crescentlabs.com>
To: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood.com>
Cc: Priya Rao <p.rao@crescentlabs.com>
Date: 2026-01-15T09:02:00-05:00
Subject: Private deployment — network ingress options

Jonas,

Thanks for taking this. High level: Crescent Labs is getting close to a private deployment pilot with Redwood in us-east-1. A couple of non-negotiables from our infra/security teams:
- P50 latency from our app fleet to inference endpoints should be < 10ms and P95 < 20ms for typical 512-token requests.
- Auditability: we need clear flow logs and per-request tracing for an upcoming audit window.
- Data residency stays in our VPC; no public internet exposure.

We'd like your recommendation between three ingress patterns: VPC Peering (cross-account), AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoint / service), and a Site-to-Site (S2S) VPN tunnel from our datacenter. Important constraints: limited ops headcount on our side (so low-maintenance is preferred), potential need for a fallback path during incidents, and we may later want to co-locate a small on-prem inference cache.

I've attached a short requirements spreadsheet and a rough network diagram. Can you outline pros/cons and a pragmatic pilot plan? Also happy to set up a short design call — Priya is the network owner.

Attachments: crescent_requirements.xlsx (requirements sheet), network-drawings-v1.pdf (high-level diagram)

Thanks,
Alex Soto
Platform Engineer — Crescent Labs
From: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood.com>
To: Alex Soto <alex.soto@crescentlabs.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>, Evelyn Hart <evelyn.hart@redwood.com>, Priya Rao <p.rao@crescentlabs.com>
Date: 2026-01-16T11:15:00-05:00
Subject: Re: Private deployment — network ingress options

Alex / Priya — thanks for the context and the attachments, clear and helpful. Looping in Ben and Kim from Solutions/Networking to do a short analysis and propose a pragmatic pilot. High-level I want to call out two possible approaches:

1) PrivateLink-first: Redwood exposes an interface endpoint (service consumer/producer model) — minimal route-table changes on Crescent's side, strong isolation, and good access controls. Slightly higher hop-count but better security posture.

2) Peering-first: VPC peering gives the lowest single-digit ms latency inside the cloud but has routing/scale caveats across accounts and limited DNS/service discovery without additional setup.

3) S2S VPN: works well for on-prem connectivity and as a fallback, but can have higher jitter and throughput limits depending on Crescent's appliance.

Ben/Kim — would you two take a pass on a short matrix (latency, ops, security, observability, cost) and recommend a pilot that proves perf and auditing? Preferably with a 2-week test window and an SLA for failover behaviors.

I can then summarize back to Crescent with a proposed schedule and a contact list for trialing routes.

Best,
Jonas Weber
Senior Solutions Architect — Redwood Inference
From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
To: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>
Cc: Alex Soto <alex.soto@crescentlabs.com>, Priya Rao <p.rao@crescentlabs.com>, Evelyn Hart <evelyn.hart@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-01-18T14:30:00-05:00
Subject: RE: Private deployment — network ingress options (tradeoffs + pilot plan)

Team / Crescent,

I ran a concise matrix and a suggested pilot approach below. Kept it practical — this is what we've executed successfully on similar pilots.

Tradeoff matrix (short):
- VPC Peering (cross-account):
  * Latency: Best (lowest RTT inside cloud). Typical added latency < 2ms if same AZ/region and well-provisioned.
  * Ops: Medium — requires careful route table management, no transitive routing, and potential CIDR overlap planning.
  * Security: Good, but lacks endpoint-level isolation; all traffic is routable across peered subnets unless NACLs/security groups restrict it.
  * Observability: VPC Flow Logs + ENIs, but you need cross-account log aggregation for centralized auditing.
  * Cost: Data transfer costs apply (regional data transfer), generally lower than PrivateLink per-GB but depends on direction.
  * When to pick: ultra-low-latency use cases where both sides are cloud-first and can coordinate CIDR/route changes.

- AWS PrivateLink (Interface Endpoint / Endpoint Service):
  * Latency: Slightly higher (~2–8ms extra depending on path and ENI placement) vs peering due to ENI/service hop. P95 could still be under your 20ms target in us-east-1 for 512-token workloads.
  * Ops: Low — Crescent only creates interface endpoints in their VPC and we manage the service. No route table surgery.
  * Security: Strong — service-level isolation, endpoint policies, and easier to restrict access per-subnet. Fits well with compliance expectations.
  * Observability: Good, but requires instrumentation on the service side. Flow logs on ENIs are available; we provide request-level tracing from the runtime.
  * Cost: Per-hour endpoint + per-GB processed; can be higher than peering for heavy sustained egress.
  * When to pick: regulated workloads where isolation/least-privilege and low operational surface are priorities.

- Site-to-Site VPN (IPSec):
  * Latency: Highest and most variable — dependent on customer appliance and internet path unless using Direct Connect. Expect added jitter; P95 might exceed 20ms depending on setup.
  * Ops: Medium-High — tunnel management, rekeying, monitoring, and appliance compatibility.
  * Security: Strong if configured correctly (IPSec + MFA controls), but wider blast radius if the on-prem network is tiered.
  * Observability: More effort — need to stitch logs from the appliance and cloud side.
  * Cost: Low fixed cloud cost but potentially higher on customer's appliance bandwidth lines.
  * When to pick: customers with strict on-prem-only rules or where private connectivity must traverse corporate DCs. Great fallback path.

Recommendation (practical):
- Primary: AWS PrivateLink (Interface Endpoint service) as the initial pattern. Rationale: meets Crescent's low ops/headcount requirement, strong isolation for audits, and will almost certainly hit your P95 20ms target in-region for standard instances.
- Fallback/Complement: Establish an S2S VPN from Crescent to a Redwood transit VPC for administrative/back-channel access and as a failover. This avoids exposing management traffic over the primary path and gives you a separate plane for troubleshooting.
- Optional: If after performance testing you find PrivateLink P95 is borderline for specific AZs/tenants, spin up a scoped VPC Peering test between the two accounts in a single AZ to validate the delta. If gains justify the complexity, we can expand.

Pilot plan (2–3 weeks):
1) Week 0 (prep): exchange CIDRs, IAM principals, and endpoint policies. Crescent shares test CIDR block and test app endpoint list.
2) Week 1 (PrivateLink smoke + perf): Crescent creates interface endpoints in a couple of subnets; Redwood publishes endpoint service with tight policy. Run perf tests (ping, 1k simulated requests) to measure P50/P95 latency and tail latency under 50/100 reqs/sec. Collect flow logs and request traces.
3) Week 2 (S2S + failover tests): Stand up VPN to transit VPC. Test failover scenarios (bring down interface ENI on our side, route shift). Measure failover detection time and request loss.
4) Week 3 (optional peering A/B test): If needed, establish a scoped VPC peering between specific subnets to measure raw latency delta.

Deliverables: perf numbers (P50/P95), flow logs capture, runbook for failover, cost estimate for 3-node pilot.

Estimated cost signal: PrivateLink will show a higher per-GB line item; peering shows up as regional data transfer. For the pilot, expect PrivateLink egress of ~$200–600 depending on traffic shape (we'll provide a narrower estimate once we have expected RPS).

Questions for Crescent (Priya/Alex):
- Do you have a preferred CIDR for a test-only VPC (small /24 is fine)?
- Any hard constraints on per-call encryption or mutual TLS you require beyond what was in the spreadsheet?
- Who on your network team will be the point for VPN termination testing?

I'll also attach a short checklist and a perf script you can run (we'll upload to the shared Drive after alignment).

-Ben
Ben Carter
Network Solutions Lead — Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Private deployment — network ingress options (proposal & next steps)

Alex / Priya — thanks for the quick turn. Based on Ben's analysis we propose the following path forward that balances your audit/ops needs with performance risk mitigation:

1) Execute PrivateLink-first pilot (2 weeks): Redwood will publish an interface endpoint service in us-east-1; Crescent will create interface endpoints in two AZs (one primary, one standby). We will instrument request-level tracing and share flow logs into your SIEM for the pilot window.

2) Establish S2S VPN to our transit VPC as a management/failover channel: this will be configured but kept out of production traffic unless we trigger failover.

3) Measure: during the pilot we'll run the perf suite Ben outlined (P50/P95/Tail under 50–100 RPS). If PrivateLink meets your SLOs we keep it as the primary. If P95 margin is tight in a targeted AZ, we'll run a scoped VPC peering experiment for that AZ to quantify actual user impact.

Action items for Crescent: please share (by end of week):
- Test CIDR block to reserve (example: 10.110.0.0/24)
- Network contact for VPN termination (name, email, preferred appliance)
- Any additional compliance artifacts you want captured in the runbook (e.g., packet-capture retention rules)

Proposed calendar: kickoff next Tue (2026-01-27) for 30 minutes to exchange artifacts and confirm test windows. I'll send a calendar invite once you confirm availability.

If that sounds good we'll prepare the internal runbook and a cost-light estimation for the pilot.

Thanks,
Jonas Weber
Senior Solutions Architect — Redwood Inference
